title: What machine learning actually is
summary: The shift from writing rules to learning patterns from data — and the three families that follow.
lead: Traditional software is a set of rules you write by hand: given an input, you spell out exactly what to do. Machine learning flips that. Instead of writing the rules, you show the computer many examples and let it infer the rules itself. You supply data and the desired answers, and the system tunes its internal numbers until its predictions match.

p: Almost everything in ML falls into three buckets. Knowing which one you're in tells you what data you need and how to measure success.

Supervised learning learns from labelled examples — emails marked spam or not-spam — to predict labels for new inputs. Unsupervised learning finds structure in unlabelled data, like clustering users by behaviour. Reinforcement learning learns by trial and reward, the way a game-playing agent improves by scoring.

A model has two phases with very different costs. Training is the expensive, one-off (or periodic) process of fitting the model to data. Inference is using the trained model to answer new questions — cheap, fast, and what your users actually hit.
As a web developer you'll mostly consume inference through an API. You rarely train large models yourself; you call one and shape its inputs and outputs.

A model that memorises its training data but fails on new data is overfitting. To catch this you split data into a training set and a held-out test set, and only trust scores on data the model has never seen.
This is the single most important habit in ML: never judge a model on the data it learned from.
key: ML learns rules from examples instead of you coding them
Pick the family — supervised, unsupervised, reinforcement — by your data
Always evaluate on held-out data, never the training set

takeaways: ML replaces hand-written rules with patterns learned from data
Training is costly and occasional; inference is cheap and constant
Overfitting is the default failure — guard against it with a test set

title: Embeddings and vector similarity
summary: How models turn words, images and documents into coordinates you can compare with maths.
lead: An embedding is a list of numbers — a vector — that represents a piece of content as a point in space. Models are trained so that things with similar meaning land near each other. "Dog" and "puppy" sit close together; "dog" and "invoice" sit far apart. That single idea powers search, recommendations and retrieval for AI apps.

p: Once text is a vector, "how similar are these two things?" becomes a geometry question. The usual measure is cosine similarity: the angle between two vectors. A small angle means similar meaning; a right angle means unrelated.
Crucially this captures meaning, not keywords. A search for "car" can surface a document about "automobiles" even with no shared words, because their vectors are close.
To add semantic search to an app: embed every document once and store the vectors; at query time, embed the user's question and find the nearest stored vectors.
In Postgres with the pgvector extension this is a single indexed query:
sections.code:
-- store
INSERT INTO docs (body, embedding) VALUES ($1, $2);

-- search: nearest neighbours to the query vector
SELECT body
FROM docs
ORDER BY embedding <=> $1   -- <=> = cosine distance
LIMIT 5;

p: Embeddings are the backbone of retrieval-augmented generation, recommendation systems, deduplication and clustering. If you've wondered how a chatbot "knows" your docs, the answer almost always starts here.
warn: Embeddings from different models aren't comparable — never mix them
Re-embed everything if you change the embedding model

takeaways: An embedding maps content to a point in meaning-space
Cosine similarity turns 'how alike?' into a fast geometry check
Embed once, store the vectors, query by nearest neighbour

title: Attention and the Transformer
summary: The mechanism behind every modern language model, explained without the heavy maths.
lead: Before Transformers, models read text strictly left to right and struggled to connect words that were far apart. The Transformer's breakthrough is attention: a way for every word to look at every other word at once and decide which ones matter for its meaning.

p: Take the sentence "the trophy didn't fit in the case because it was too big." What does "it" refer to? Attention lets the model weight "trophy" heavily and "case" lightly when interpreting "it". Each word builds its representation by pulling in context from the words it attends to.
Self-attention runs this for every word simultaneously, which is why Transformers parallelise so well on GPUs.

A Transformer stacks many attention layers. Early layers capture local grammar; deeper layers capture abstract meaning and long-range structure. Stack enough of them, train on enough text, and surprisingly general capabilities emerge.
The model only ever predicts the next token. Everything you see in a chatbot is that simple objective, repeated, at scale.

Two practical consequences fall out of this design. First, the context window — how many tokens the model can attend to at once — is finite and costs grow with it. Second, the model has no memory between calls; you must resend context each time.
key: Attention lets every token weigh every other token
Depth plus scale is where general capability emerges
Finite context and no built-in memory shape how you build apps

takeaways: Attention connects any two tokens directly, regardless of distance
Models just predict the next token — capability comes from scale
Context windows are finite and stateless; you manage memory yourself

title: Prompt engineering that actually works
summary: A handful of reliable techniques that move model output from flaky to dependable.
lead: Prompting is the interface to a model, and small changes produce large differences in quality. You don't need tricks — you need clarity, structure and a few repeatable patterns.

sections.h: Be specific and show the shape
p: Vague prompts get vague answers. State the role, the task, the constraints and the output format explicitly. If you need machine-readable output, ask for JSON and describe the exact keys.
Giving one or two examples (few-shot) is often the single biggest quality lever — the model imitates the pattern you demonstrate.

For reasoning tasks, asking the model to work step by step before answering improves accuracy. For production you then want structure: request the reasoning and the final answer in separate fields so you can use the answer programmatically.

Temperature governs creativity. Near 0 gives focused, repeatable output — use it for classification and extraction. Higher values explore more — use them for brainstorming and copy. Match the setting to the job.
warn: Models drift — always validate JSON output before trusting it
Test prompts on edge cases, not just the happy path

takeaways: Specify role, task, constraints and exact output format
Few-shot examples and step-by-step both lift quality
Low temperature for extraction, higher for creative work

title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)
summary: Give a model your private knowledge without retraining it — the dominant pattern for AI apps.
lead: Language models only know what they were trained on, and they happily make things up when asked beyond it. RAG fixes both problems by retrieving relevant facts from your own data and handing them to the model alongside the question.

p: RAG has two phases. Offline: split your documents into chunks, embed each chunk, and store the vectors. Online: embed the user's question, retrieve the closest chunks, and place them into the prompt as context before the model answers.
The model now answers from your sources rather than its frozen training memory.

sections.h: Why it beats fine-tuning for facts
p: Fine-tuning bakes behaviour into a model but is a poor way to add fast-changing knowledge. RAG keeps your knowledge in a database you can update instantly — change a document and the next answer reflects it, no retraining.
It also gives you citations: you know exactly which chunks produced an answer.

Quality lives in retrieval. Chunk sensibly (by section, not arbitrary length), retrieve a handful of candidates, and consider re-ranking them. Instruct the model to answer only from the provided context and to say when it doesn't know.
key: Retrieve relevant chunks, then let the model answer from them
RAG adds knowledge instantly — no retraining, and you get citations
Most RAG quality problems are retrieval problems, not model problems

takeaways: RAG grounds answers in your data instead of model memory
Prefer RAG over fine-tuning for facts that change
Invest in chunking and retrieval — that's where quality comes from

title: Shipping an AI feature in a web app
summary: The architecture, the streaming UX and the security rule that separate a demo from a product.
lead: Wiring a model into a React or Next.js app is mostly ordinary web engineering with three things to get right: where the key lives, how responses reach the UI, and how you control cost.

sections.h: Keep the key on the server
p: Never call a model API directly from the browser in production — your key would be exposed to anyone who opens devtools. Put a thin server route in front of it. In Next.js that's a Route Handler that reads the key from an environment variable and forwards the request.

Models generate token by token. Waiting for the whole answer feels slow; streaming it as it arrives feels instant. Forward the server-sent events from your route to the client and append tokens as they land. TanStack Query or the Vercel AI SDK handle the plumbing.

Treat the model like any unreliable, metered dependency. Cache repeated prompts, set sensible token limits, add timeouts and retries, and show graceful fallbacks. Log token usage so cost never surprises you.
warn: A client-side API key is the most common AI-app security mistake
Always handle timeouts, rate limits and partial failures

takeaways: Proxy the model through a server route so the key stays private
Stream tokens to the UI for an instant, responsive feel
Cache, cap tokens and monitor usage to keep cost predictable

title: Foundation models and LLMs
summary: What a large language model is, why 'foundation model' is the better name, and how scale changed everything.
lead: A large language model is a neural network trained on a vast amount of text to predict the next token. From that single objective — guess what comes next — surprisingly general capabilities emerge: summarising, translating, writing code, and reasoning step by step. The phrase 'foundation model' captures the bigger idea: one model, pre-trained once at great cost, that you then adapt to countless downstream tasks instead of training a fresh model per task.

p: Models read and write in tokens — chunks of text roughly three-quarters of a word on average. Both your input and the model's output are counted in tokens, which is what you pay for and what the context window measures.
Thinking in tokens explains odd behaviour: a model may miscount letters in a word because it never sees letters, only tokens.

Performance improved predictably as models, data, and compute grew together — the 'scaling laws'. Past certain sizes, abilities the model was never explicitly taught (in-context learning, chain-of-thought) appeared.
This is why a handful of labs train enormous base models and everyone else builds on top via APIs, fine-tuning, or open weights.
key: An LLM predicts the next token; broad skills emerge from that
'Foundation model' = pre-train once, adapt many times
You are billed in tokens for both prompt and completion

takeaways: LLMs are next-token predictors whose generality emerges from scale
Everything is measured in tokens, not words
Foundation models are adapted, not retrained, for each use

title: Reading the model landscape
summary: How to compare today's models without memorising leaderboards that change monthly.
lead: New models ship constantly, so the durable skill is knowing the axes to compare them on rather than today's rankings. Frontier proprietary models (from labs like OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google) trade off against strong open-weight families (such as Llama, Mistral, and Qwen) you can self-host. The right choice depends on capability, cost, latency, context length, and whether you need to run it on your own infrastructure.

p: Compare on: raw capability for your task, price per million tokens, latency, context-window size, multimodality, and licensing. A cheaper, faster model that is 'good enough' often beats a frontier model for high-volume work.
Open weights give you control, privacy, and no per-token fee, at the cost of running and scaling the infrastructure yourself.
Mature apps route: a small fast model handles easy requests and escalates hard ones to a frontier model. This controls cost without sacrificing quality where it counts.
Because specifics shift fast, benchmark on your own data and re-check periodically rather than trusting a single public leaderboard.
warn: Model names, prices, and rankings change frequently — verify against current docs before committing

takeaways: Compare on capability, cost, latency, context, and licensing
Open weights trade convenience for control and privacy
Route easy work to small models, hard work to frontier models

title: Context windows and context engineering
summary: The context window is the model's working memory — and managing what goes in it is now a core skill.
lead: A model has no memory between calls; everything it 'knows' in a request must fit inside its context window — the maximum number of tokens it can attend to at once. Context engineering is the discipline of deciding what to put in that window: instructions, retrieved documents, conversation history, tool results, and examples. Get it right and the model is sharp and grounded; get it wrong and it hallucinates or ignores what matters.

p: Long-context models can accept hundreds of thousands of tokens, but stuffing the window degrades quality and raises cost and latency. Models attend unevenly — the middle of a very long context is often neglected, a pattern sometimes called 'lost in the middle'.
Curate ruthlessly: include the few things the model needs for this turn, not everything you have.
Put instructions and the most important material near the start or end. Summarise or trim old conversation. Retrieve only the most relevant chunks rather than whole documents.
Treat the window as a budget you actively spend, not a bucket you fill.
key: The context window is the model's only working memory
More tokens means more cost, latency, and dilution
Curate and position context deliberately

takeaways: Everything the model knows for a request lives in the context window
Long context still rewards careful curation
Position and trim context like a budget

title: Fine-tuning vs prompting vs RAG
summary: Three ways to adapt a model to your needs — and when each is the right tool.
lead: When a base model is not quite doing what you want, you have three levers: prompt it better, give it knowledge via retrieval, or fine-tune its weights. They solve different problems and are frequently combined. Reaching for fine-tuning first is a common and expensive mistake.

sections.h: Match the lever to the gap
p: If the model lacks facts, use RAG. If it has the knowledge but not the format, tone, or behaviour you want, prompt better or fine-tune. Prompting is the cheapest, fastest, and most reversible — exhaust it first.
Fine-tuning teaches style and structure, not new facts; do not fine-tune to inject knowledge that changes over time.
A production system might use a fine-tuned model for consistent format, RAG for current facts, and a carefully engineered prompt to tie them together.
Start simple, measure, and add complexity only when the metric demands it.
key: Prompting: cheapest, try first
RAG: for facts and freshness
Fine-tuning: for behaviour, tone, and format — not knowledge

takeaways: Diagnose the gap before choosing a lever
Fine-tuning shapes behaviour, RAG supplies knowledge
Prompt first; combine techniques as needed

title: Evaluating LLM apps (evals)
summary: If you cannot measure your AI feature, you cannot improve it — evals are the test suite for non-deterministic systems.
lead: Traditional tests assume the same input gives the same output. LLMs are probabilistic, so you need a different safety net: evals, a curated set of inputs with a way to score the outputs. Without them, every prompt or model change is a guess, and regressions slip through silently.

p: Build a dataset of representative cases with expected qualities. Score with exact checks where possible, and use an LLM-as-judge or human review for open-ended quality. Track the score over time like any other metric.
Even a few dozen good cases beat vibes-based testing.
Run evals in CI so prompt and model changes are gated by measured quality, not opinion. Log production traces and feed failures back into the eval set.
Treat evals as a living asset that grows with every bug you find.
key: Evals are tests for probabilistic systems
Mix exact checks, LLM-as-judge, and human review
Gate changes on measured quality, not intuition

takeaways: LLM apps need evals because outputs vary
A small, representative dataset beats ad-hoc checking
Run evals in CI and grow them from real failures

title: Multimodal models
summary: Models that see, hear, and read — and what that unlocks for your apps.
lead: Modern frontier models are increasingly multimodal: a single model can accept text alongside images, audio, or even video, and reason across them. Under the hood, each modality is turned into tokens in a shared representation, so the model treats a picture much like a paragraph.

p: Describe or answer questions about an image, transcribe and reason over audio, extract structured data from screenshots or documents, or generate images and speech. One API call can mix a question with a photo.
This collapses pipelines that used to need separate OCR, vision, and speech services.
Images and audio consume many tokens, so multimodal requests can be expensive — size and crop inputs sensibly. Quality varies by modality and model.
Validate critical extractions; a confident wrong answer about a document is still wrong.
key: One model can reason across text, images, and audio
Each modality becomes tokens in a shared space
Media inputs are token-heavy — manage cost

takeaways: Multimodal models unify text, vision, and audio
They replace several single-purpose services
Watch token cost and verify critical outputs

title: Quantization, distillation and local models
summary: How big models are shrunk to run cheaply — on a server you control or even a laptop.
lead: Frontier models are huge, but you rarely need their full size. Two techniques make models smaller and cheaper: quantization stores the model's numbers at lower precision, and distillation trains a small 'student' model to imitate a large 'teacher'. Together with open weights, they let capable models run on modest hardware.

p: Weights are usually 16-bit floats; quantizing to 8-bit or 4-bit roughly halves or quarters memory with modest quality loss. It is the single most practical lever for fitting a model on a given GPU.
Tools and runtimes make running quantized open models locally straightforward.
A distilled model captures much of a larger model's behaviour at a fraction of the size and cost, ideal for high-volume, latency-sensitive tasks.
The trade is capability for efficiency — benchmark the small model on your task before shipping.
key: Quantization lowers numeric precision to save memory
Distillation trains small models to mimic large ones
Both trade some quality for big cost and speed wins

takeaways: Quantization and distillation shrink models for cheap inference
Open weights plus these techniques enable local deployment
Always benchmark the smaller model on your real task

title: How React rendering really works
summary: Render, commit and re-render — the cycle that explains most React performance questions.
lead: A lot of React confusion clears up once you separate two things React does: figuring out what the UI should look like (render) and actually changing the DOM (commit). Rendering is calling your component function; it's cheap and happens often. Commit is touching the real DOM; React does the minimum it can.

p: A component re-renders when its state changes, when its parent re-renders, or when a context it consumes changes. That's it. When a component re-renders, all of its children re-render by default — even if their props didn't change.
This default is usually fine. React is fast. Problems appear only when a frequently-changing parent sits above an expensive subtree.

After rendering, React diffs the new tree against the old one and applies only the differences. In lists it matches items by their key. A stable, unique key lets React move and reuse DOM nodes; using an array index as a key breaks this when the list reorders, causing subtle state bugs.

Before reaching for memoisation, find the actual culprit with the Profiler. Often the fix is structural: move state down so fewer components re-render, or lift expensive children out as props so they don't re-render with the parent.
key: Render is cheap and frequent; commit touches the DOM and is minimal
Children re-render with their parent unless you intervene
Give list items stable keys — never the array index for dynamic lists

takeaways: Separate render (calling your function) from commit (DOM changes)
State, parent renders and context changes drive re-renders
Profile first; restructure before you memoise

title: useMemo, useCallback and the cost of re-renders
summary: When memoisation genuinely helps, when it's noise, and how to tell the difference.
lead: useMemo caches a computed value and useCallback caches a function, both recomputing only when their dependencies change. They exist to skip expensive work and to keep references stable across renders. They are not free, and sprinkling them everywhere makes code slower to read and sometimes slower to run.

p: Reach for useMemo when a calculation is genuinely expensive — sorting a large list, heavy data transforms. Reach for useCallback (or useMemo) when a value is passed to a memoised child or used in a dependency array, where a fresh reference each render would defeat the optimisation downstream.

Every memo has a cost: React stores the value and compares dependencies each render. For a cheap calculation that cost can exceed the work you're avoiding. And a memo around a component does nothing if you keep handing it new object or function props inline.

Write the straightforward version first. Memoise only when the Profiler shows a real cost, or when you're deliberately stabilising a reference for React.memo or a hook dependency. Measure, don't guess.
warn: Memoising trivial values often costs more than it saves
React.memo is useless if parents pass new inline props each render

takeaways: useMemo caches values, useCallback caches functions
Use them for expensive work or to stabilise references
Default to the simple version; memoise only when profiling justifies it

title: Server state with TanStack Query
summary: Why server data deserves its own tool instead of useState plus useEffect.
lead: Most app state isn't really client state — it's a cached copy of data that lives on a server. Treating it like local state with useState and useEffect forces you to hand-roll caching, loading flags, refetching and invalidation. TanStack Query gives you all of that as a small, declarative hook.

p: You describe the data with a query key and a function that fetches it. The library handles caching, deduping identical requests, background refetching and exposing loading and error states.

Writes go through useMutation. After a successful write you invalidate the relevant query keys, and any component showing that data refetches automatically. Optimistic updates let the UI respond instantly and roll back if the server rejects the change.

The payoff is consistency: the same data shown in three places stays in sync from one cache, and you stop writing the same fetch-loading-error boilerplate in every component. It pairs naturally with an AI backend route — wrap your /api/ai call in a query or mutation and you get retries and caching for free.

takeaways: Server data is cached remote state, not local state
Query keys drive caching, deduping and background refetch
Invalidate keys after mutations to keep the UI consistent

title: useEffect and the rules of hooks
summary: Why hooks must follow two rules, and why useEffect is the one most often misused.
lead: Hooks let function components hold state and side effects, but they rely on call order, so they come with two rules: only call hooks at the top level, and only from React functions. Break them and React loses track of which state is which. useEffect, in particular, is reached for too often.

p: Never call a hook inside a condition, loop, or nested function — call them unconditionally at the top of the component so their order is stable across renders. Only call them from components or custom hooks.
A linter enforces these; trust it.

useEffect is for synchronising with systems outside React — subscriptions, the DOM, network. It is not for transforming data during render or responding to events; those belong in event handlers or derived values.
If an effect's only job is to compute state from props, you usually do not need it.
key: Call hooks unconditionally, at the top level
useEffect is for external synchronisation, not data shaping
Many effects can be replaced by derived values or handlers

takeaways: Hooks depend on stable call order — follow the two rules
useEffect synchronises with the outside world
Avoid effects for work that belongs in render or handlers

title: App Router vs Pages Router
summary: The model shift behind Next.js's App Router and when each router fits.
lead: Next.js ships two routing systems. The older Pages Router maps files in /pages to routes and runs components on the client by default. The newer App Router, built on React Server Components, makes components run on the server by default and treats data fetching as a first-class, server-side concern.

p: In the App Router, a component is a Server Component unless you mark it with "use client". Server Components run on the server, can fetch data directly (even hit a database), and send zero JavaScript for themselves to the browser. You opt into client interactivity only where you need state or effects.

The App Router introduces nested layouts that persist across navigation, loading and error boundaries per route segment, and streaming so parts of a page can render before slower data arrives. This structure removes a lot of boilerplate the Pages Router required.

For new projects the App Router is the default direction and unlocks server components, streaming and server actions. The Pages Router remains fully supported and is reasonable for existing apps or simpler sites; the two can even coexist during migration.
key: App Router components run on the server unless marked 'use client'
Nested layouts, streaming and error boundaries are built in
New projects start with App Router; Pages Router is still supported

takeaways: App Router defaults to server components; Pages Router to client
Server components fetch data directly and ship no JS themselves
Choose App Router for new work; both can coexist while migrating

title: SSR, SSG and ISR — choosing a strategy
summary: When a page should render — at build, on each request, or somewhere in between.
lead: Next.js lets each route pick when its HTML is produced. Getting this choice right is the difference between a fast, cheap site and a slow, expensive one. The three classic strategies trade freshness against speed and cost.

p: Static Generation (SSG) renders the page at build time — fastest and cheapest, perfect for content that rarely changes like docs or marketing pages. Server Rendering (SSR) renders on every request — always fresh, ideal for personalised or rapidly-changing pages, but more work per visit. Incremental Static Regeneration (ISR) serves a static page but regenerates it in the background on a schedule, blending static speed with periodic freshness.

You rarely pick one for the whole app. A blog index might be ISR, an article static, a dashboard server-rendered. Decide per route by asking: how fresh must this be, and how expensive is it to render?
In the App Router these strategies are expressed through caching and revalidation. Understanding what's cached, for how long, and how to invalidate it is what actually determines freshness and cost.
warn: Over-using force-dynamic throws away caching and raises cost
Stale data usually means a missing revalidation, not a bug

takeaways: SSG = build time, SSR = per request, ISR = static with background refresh
Pick a strategy per route based on freshness vs cost
In App Router this is all expressed through caching and revalidation

title: Server Actions, end to end
summary: Call server code straight from a component — mutations without hand-writing an API layer.
lead: A Server Action is an async function that runs on the server but can be called directly from your components, including from a form. It removes the ceremony of defining an API route, fetching it, and wiring up the request just to save a value.

p: Mark a function with "use server". You can pass it to a form's action or call it from a client component. Next.js handles the network round-trip for you.

After a mutation you call revalidatePath or revalidateTag so the affected pages rebuild with fresh data. This is the server-side equivalent of invalidating a query cache — the user sees the update without a manual refetch.

Server Actions run real server code, so treat their inputs as untrusted: validate everything and enforce authorisation inside the action. The smooth developer experience can tempt you to skip the checks you'd never skip in an API route.
warn: Validate and authorise every Server Action input — it's a real endpoint
Don't expose secrets in client components that call actions

takeaways: Server Actions let components call server code without a manual API
Pair them with revalidatePath/Tag to refresh cached data
They're real endpoints — validate inputs and check auth

title: React Server Components in Next.js
summary: The default in the App Router: components that run on the server and ship zero JavaScript to the browser.
lead: In the Next.js App Router, components are Server Components by default. They render on the server, can fetch data directly, and send only HTML to the client — no component JavaScript. You opt into interactivity explicitly with a 'use client' directive, keeping the interactive surface small.

sections.h: Server by default, client on demand
p: Server Components can await data inline and access server resources, but cannot use state or effects. When you need interactivity — onClick, useState — add 'use client' at the top of that file.
The skill is drawing the boundary: keep most of the tree on the server and push 'use client' to the leaves.
Less shipped JavaScript means faster loads. Data fetching moves next to the components that use it, and secrets stay on the server.
Server Actions extend this by letting client components call server functions directly for mutations.
key: Components are Server Components unless marked 'use client'
Server Components fetch data inline and ship no JS
Push interactivity to the leaves of the tree

takeaways: The App Router defaults to server rendering with zero client JS
'use client' opts a subtree into interactivity
Keep the client boundary small for performance

title: Generics that earn their keep
summary: Write functions and types that stay flexible without losing type safety.
lead: Generics let a function or type work over many types while preserving the relationships between them. The classic example: a function that returns whatever type it receives, so the caller keeps full type information instead of collapsing to any.

p: Without generics you either lose safety (any) or duplicate code per type. A generic captures the connection — input type relates to output type — so the compiler can check it everywhere.
Unbounded generics can't do much — you don't know anything about T. Constrain them with extends to require a shape, which unlocks property access while staying generic.
Generics are a tool for genuine reuse, not a badge of sophistication. If a function only ever handles one type, a generic adds noise. Add them when two or more types must move together.
warn: A generic with no constraint and no relationship is just noise
If you find yourself casting inside a generic, the design is off

takeaways: Generics preserve type relationships across many types
Constrain with extends to safely use a type's shape
Use them for real reuse, not decoration

title: Discriminated unions and exhaustive checks
summary: Model 'one of several shapes' precisely, and let the compiler force you to handle every case.
lead: A discriminated union is a set of object types that share a common literal field — the discriminant — which tells them apart. It's the most reliable way to model state that can be in exactly one of several shapes, like a request that is loading, succeeded or failed.

p: Give each variant a shared tag field with a unique literal value. TypeScript then narrows the type when you check that field.
Add a never-typed default and the compiler errors the day someone adds a new variant they forgot to handle. This turns a whole class of runtime bugs into compile-time errors.

Modelling state with separate booleans (isLoading, isError) allows impossible combinations like loading and error at once. A discriminated union makes those states unrepresentable, which is the whole goal of good typing.
key: A shared literal field lets TS narrow to one variant
A never default forces you to handle every case
Unions make impossible states impossible — better than boolean flags

takeaways: Discriminated unions model 'one of N shapes' precisely
Checking the discriminant narrows the type automatically
A never check gives compile-time exhaustiveness

title: The Node event loop, demystified
summary: How a single thread handles thousands of connections — and what blocks it.
lead: Node runs your JavaScript on a single thread, yet serves huge numbers of concurrent connections. The trick is the event loop: rather than waiting for slow operations like disk or network, Node hands them off and keeps working, picking up the results via callbacks when they're ready.

p: When you read a file or query a database, Node delegates the wait to the operating system and immediately moves on. The event loop continuously checks for completed operations and runs their callbacks. Your code never sits idle waiting.

sections.h: What ruins it: blocking the thread
p: Because there's one thread for your JavaScript, any synchronous CPU-heavy work freezes everything — every other request stalls until it finishes. A tight loop, synchronous crypto, or huge JSON parsing can take the whole server down in latency.

The event loop is brilliant for I/O-bound work but uses one CPU core. To use all cores, run multiple processes (the cluster module or a process manager) or offload heavy computation to worker threads.
warn: Synchronous CPU work blocks all requests — keep hot paths async
One event loop = one core; scale with processes or workers

takeaways: Node offloads slow I/O and processes results via the event loop
One JS thread means synchronous heavy work blocks everything
Scale across cores with clustering or worker threads

title: Streams and backpressure
summary: Process data piece by piece instead of loading it all into memory.
lead: A stream lets you handle data incrementally — a chunk at a time — rather than buffering an entire file or response in memory. For large payloads this is the difference between a steady, low-memory server and one that falls over under load.

p: Reading a 2GB file into a variable to send it will exhaust memory. Streaming reads and writes a little at a time, keeping memory flat regardless of size.

If a fast source feeds a slow destination, data piles up. Backpressure is the mechanism by which the destination tells the source to slow down. pipe() handles it for you; if you wire streams manually, you must respect it or memory creeps up.

HTTP request and response bodies are streams. So are file reads, compression, and crucially the token-by-token output of an AI model. Forwarding a model's streamed response to your client is just piping one stream into another.
key: Streams process data in chunks with flat memory use
Backpressure stops a fast producer overwhelming a slow consumer
HTTP bodies and AI token streams are streams you can pipe

takeaways: Stream large data instead of buffering it into memory
Respect backpressure so producers don't outrun consumers
Request/response bodies and AI output are all streams

title: Caching strategies that scale
summary: Where to put a cache, how to keep it fresh, and the failure modes to plan for.
lead: Caching trades a little staleness for a lot of speed and cost saving by keeping a copy of expensive-to-produce data close to where it's needed. The hard part isn't storing the copy — it's deciding when it's allowed to be wrong, and for how long.

p: Caches stack from client to database: the browser, a CDN at the edge, an in-memory store like Redis in front of your services, and the database's own buffers. A request ideally never reaches the slow layers because a faster one already has the answer.

The classic pattern is cache-aside: check the cache, and on a miss load from the database and populate the cache with a time-to-live. Freshness comes from expiry plus explicit invalidation when the underlying data changes. Naming what to invalidate is the part teams underestimate.

When a popular cached item expires, many requests can miss at once and all hammer the database — a cache stampede. Mitigate with slightly randomised expiry, a lock so only one request refills, or serving stale data while a single refresh happens in the background.
warn: The hardest cache bug is invalidation — decide it up front
Synchronised expiry causes stampedes; jitter your TTLs

takeaways: Cache in layers from browser to CDN to Redis to the database
Cache-aside with TTL plus invalidation is the workhorse pattern
Design for stampedes with jittered TTLs and single-flight refills

title: Designing a URL shortener
summary: A compact interview classic that exercises IDs, storage, caching and scale.
lead: A URL shortener takes a long URL and returns a short code that redirects to it. It looks trivial, which is why it's a great lens on system design: every interesting decision — how to generate codes, how to store them, how to make redirects fast — shows up in miniature.

p: You need a short, unique key per URL. Two common approaches: encode an auto-incrementing ID into base62 (short, ordered, but guessable), or generate a random code and check for collisions (unguessable, slightly more work). Base62 of a counter gives you billions of codes in six characters.

Shorteners are overwhelmingly reads — one create, many redirects. So optimise the redirect path ruthlessly: a key-value store keyed by code, fronted by a cache, returns the long URL in microseconds. Writes can afford to be slower.

Once the basics work, the follow-ups reveal depth: analytics on clicks, custom aliases, expiry, rate limiting to stop abuse, and global low latency via edge caching. Each maps to a real distributed-systems concern.
key: Base62 of an ID, or random-with-collision-check, makes the code
Redirects dominate — cache the code-to-URL lookup aggressively
Analytics, expiry and rate limiting are where the real design lives

takeaways: Short codes come from base62 IDs or checked random strings
The system is read-heavy — make redirects cache-fast
Analytics, abuse control and edge latency add the real depth

title: AWS core building blocks
summary: The handful of services that underpin almost every AWS architecture.
lead: AWS has hundreds of services, but most applications stand on a small core. Learn these well and the rest slot into place as variations and specialisations.

p: EC2 gives you virtual machines you manage yourself — maximum control, maximum responsibility. Lambda runs your code in response to events with no servers to manage and pay-per-invocation pricing; ideal for glue, APIs and bursty workloads. Containers sit between, via ECS or EKS.

S3 is durable object storage for files, backups and static assets — effectively infinite and cheap. RDS runs managed relational databases (Postgres, MySQL) so you don't babysit servers. DynamoDB is a managed key-value and document store for predictable low-latency access at scale.

A VPC is your private network in the cloud, controlling what can talk to what. IAM governs who and what can perform which actions — the backbone of AWS security. Most real-world AWS incidents trace back to misconfigured IAM or networking, so these repay careful study.
key: EC2 for control, Lambda for serverless, containers in between
S3 for objects, RDS for relational, DynamoDB for key-value at scale
VPC and IAM control connectivity and permissions — learn them deeply

takeaways: A small core — compute, storage, networking — covers most apps
Lambda removes server management; EC2 keeps full control
VPC and IAM are where security is won or lost

title: AWS and the Well-Architected mindset
summary: Navigating AWS's huge service catalog with a framework instead of memorising names.
lead: AWS offers hundreds of services, which is overwhelming without a mental map. Group them by job — compute, storage, database, networking, security — and lean on the Well-Architected Framework's pillars to make decisions rather than memorising every product.

p: Compute runs code (EC2, Lambda, ECS); storage holds data (S3, EBS); databases manage it (RDS, DynamoDB); networking connects it (VPC, CloudFront); and IAM governs who can do what.
IAM and least-privilege permissions underpin everything you build.
Well-Architected names five concerns — operational excellence, security, reliability, performance efficiency, and cost optimisation — to weigh in any design.
Use them as a checklist when choosing services and configurations.
key: Group services by compute, storage, database, networking
IAM and least privilege govern access
Weigh designs against the Well-Architected pillars

takeaways: Map AWS services by the job they do
IAM and least privilege are foundational
Use Well-Architected pillars to guide decisions

title: Docker images and layers
summary: Why containers are reproducible, and how layer caching makes builds fast.
lead: A container packages your application with everything it needs to run — runtime, libraries, config — so it behaves identically on your laptop, in CI, and in production. The recipe for a container is an image, and understanding how images are built explains both their reliability and their build speed.

p: Each instruction in a Dockerfile creates a layer stacked on the previous one. Layers are cached and reused: if nothing in a layer or those above it changed, Docker reuses the cached version instead of rebuilding. Ordering your Dockerfile to exploit this is the main lever on build time.
sections.code:
# Copy dependency manifests first so 'npm ci' is cached
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci
# Source changes often — copy it last
COPY . .
RUN npm run build

p: If you copy all your source before installing dependencies, every code change busts the dependency cache and reinstalls everything. Copy the lockfile and install first, then copy source — now a code edit only reruns the cheap final layers.
Smaller images deploy faster and have less to attack. Use a slim base image and multi-stage builds: compile in a fat builder stage, then copy only the artefacts into a tiny runtime image.
warn: Copying source before installing deps destroys build caching
Don't ship build tools to production — use multi-stage builds

takeaways: Images are cached layers — reuse depends on what changed
Order the Dockerfile so dependencies cache and source copies last
Slim bases and multi-stage builds keep images small and safe

title: Containers and Kubernetes, demystified
summary: Why containers changed deployment, and what Kubernetes adds on top.
lead: A container packages an app with its dependencies so it runs the same everywhere, solving 'works on my machine'. Docker builds and runs containers; Kubernetes orchestrates many of them across a cluster of machines.

p: A Dockerfile defines an image — your app plus its runtime — that starts in seconds and is isolated from the host. Images are portable across laptops, CI, and production.
Containers are lightweight compared with virtual machines because they share the host kernel.
Kubernetes schedules containers (in Pods) across nodes, restarts failures, scales replicas, and routes traffic via Services. You declare the desired state, and it works to maintain it.
Its power comes with real operational complexity — adopt it when you genuinely need it.
key: Containers package app and dependencies for portability
Docker builds images; Kubernetes orchestrates them
Kubernetes maintains your declared desired state

takeaways: Containers make deployments reproducible and portable
Kubernetes schedules, heals, and scales containers
Its complexity is worth it only at real scale

title: What 'agentic AI' really means
summary: Beyond chatbots: systems that pursue a goal by taking actions, observing results, and deciding what to do next.
lead: A plain LLM call maps one input to one output. An agent wraps the model in a loop and gives it tools, so it can take actions in the world — search, call APIs, run code — observe what happened, and choose its next step toward a goal. 'Agentic' describes that shift from answering to acting.

p: The model is the reasoning engine; the agent is the scaffolding around it: a loop, a set of tools, memory, and a stopping condition. Given 'book me a meeting', an agent might check a calendar, find a slot, and send an invite across several steps.
Autonomy is a spectrum — most useful agents keep a human in the loop for consequential actions.
Reliable tool calling and larger context windows made multi-step agents practical. The hard parts are no longer 'can it reason' but 'can it stay on track, recover from errors, and stop'.
Start with the simplest design that works; agents add power and failure modes in equal measure.
key: An agent = model + loop + tools + memory + stop condition
Agentic means taking actions, not just producing text
Keep humans in the loop for consequential steps

takeaways: Agents wrap an LLM in a loop with tools and a goal
The model reasons; the scaffolding acts and observes
Favour the simplest design and human oversight

title: The agent loop: reason, act, observe
summary: The ReAct pattern — reason, act, observe, repeat — is the heartbeat of almost every agent.
lead: Most agents run a simple cycle often called ReAct: the model reasons about what to do, acts by calling a tool, observes the result, and loops with that new information until the goal is met or a limit is hit. This interleaving of thinking and doing is what lets an agent handle tasks no single prompt could.

p: The model emits a thought and a chosen action with arguments. Your code runs the tool, captures the result, and feeds it back as an observation. The model then decides whether to act again or finish.
Each observation becomes part of the context, so the agent's 'reasoning' accumulates across steps.
Set a maximum number of steps and clear stopping conditions, or an agent can loop forever or thrash. Handle tool errors as observations the model can recover from.
Log every step — traces are how you debug an agent that went off the rails.
key: ReAct = reason, act, observe, repeat
Tool results re-enter the context as observations
Always bound steps and log traces

takeaways: The agent loop interleaves reasoning with tool use
Observations accumulate in context across steps
Bound the loop and trace every step for debugging

title: Tool calling and function calling
summary: How a model that only outputs text can reliably trigger real actions in your code.
lead: Tool calling (also called function calling) is the bridge between a language model and your software. You describe the tools available — each with a name, description, and a schema for its arguments — and the model responds with a structured request to call one, filling in the arguments. Your code executes it and returns the result. This is the mechanism behind virtually every agent.

p: You pass tool definitions alongside the prompt. Instead of prose, the model can emit a JSON object naming a tool and its arguments, validated against your schema. You run the function and feed the output back.
Good tool descriptions and argument schemas matter as much as the prompt — the model chooses tools from them.
Keep each tool focused and well-named, with a description that says when to use it. Validate arguments before executing, and return errors the model can read and retry.
Fewer, sharper tools beat a sprawling toolbox the model misuses.
key: The model emits structured calls; your code executes them
Tool descriptions and schemas drive the model's choices
Validate arguments and return readable errors

takeaways: Tool calling turns model output into real actions
Schemas and descriptions are part of the prompt design
Validate inputs and make errors recoverable

title: Memory for agents
summary: Agents forget everything between runs unless you design memory — short-term and long-term.
lead: An LLM is stateless, so any continuity an agent shows is engineered. Short-term memory is the working context of the current task — recent steps and tool results held in the window. Long-term memory persists across sessions, usually in a database or vector store the agent can search. Knowing which is which prevents both forgetfulness and bloated context.

p: Recent observations and decisions stay in the context window so the agent can follow a multi-step task. Because the window is finite, you summarise or drop older steps as it grows.
This is memory you spend tokens on every turn.
Facts, preferences, and past outcomes are stored outside the model and retrieved when relevant, often via embeddings. The agent pulls in only what this task needs.
Separating the two keeps the context lean while still letting the agent 'remember' across sessions.
key: LLMs are stateless; memory is engineered
Short-term lives in the context window and is trimmed
Long-term lives in storage and is retrieved on demand

takeaways: Agent continuity is built, not inherent
Short-term memory is the trimmed working context
Long-term memory is external storage you retrieve from

title: Multi-agent systems and orchestration
summary: When one agent is not enough: dividing work among specialised agents and coordinating them.
lead: A single agent juggling many responsibilities gets confused. Multi-agent systems split the problem into focused roles — a researcher, a writer, a critic — coordinated by an orchestrator or a supervisor agent that routes work and combines results. The pattern mirrors a team with a manager.

p: A supervisor delegates subtasks to workers and assembles their output. Agents can also hand off to one another, passing control and context like a relay. Pipelines chain agents in a fixed order.
Each agent gets a smaller, clearer job, which usually beats one over-loaded generalist.
More agents means more calls, more latency, and more places to go wrong. Pass only the context each agent needs, and add a step that checks or critiques results.
Reach for multi-agent only when a single well-scoped agent genuinely cannot cope.
key: Split work into focused roles with a coordinator
Supervisors delegate; handoffs pass control
Coordination adds cost — justify the extra agents

takeaways: Multiple specialised agents beat one overloaded one
Supervisors and handoffs are the core coordination patterns
Add agents only when complexity demands it

title: Model Context Protocol (MCP)
summary: The open standard that lets any AI app plug into any tool or data source — think 'USB-C for AI'.
lead: Before MCP, every AI app wired up each tool and data source with bespoke, one-off integrations. The Model Context Protocol is an open standard that defines a common way for AI applications (clients) to connect to external capabilities (servers). Build an MCP server once, and any MCP-compatible app can use it — the same plug fits every socket.

sections.h: Clients, servers, and what they expose
p: An MCP client lives in the AI app; an MCP server wraps a capability — your database, a SaaS API, the file system. Servers expose three things: tools (actions the model can call), resources (data it can read), and prompts (reusable templates).
The model discovers what a server offers at runtime and calls it through the standard protocol.
MCP turns N apps times M tools — a combinatorial mess of custom connectors — into N plus M. Vendors ship one server; apps speak one protocol. It is rapidly becoming the default way to extend agents.
Treat MCP servers like any dependency: review their permissions and trust, since they can act on your behalf.
key: MCP standardises how AI apps connect to tools and data
Servers expose tools, resources, and prompts
Build once, reuse across every MCP-compatible client
warn: MCP servers can read data and take actions — vet their source and permissions

takeaways: MCP is an open standard for connecting AI apps to capabilities
Servers expose tools, resources, and prompts to any client
It replaces bespoke integrations with one shared protocol

title: Guardrails and human-in-the-loop
summary: Autonomy without limits is a liability — guardrails and approvals keep agents safe and useful.
lead: An agent that can act can also act wrongly: delete the wrong record, send the wrong email, spend real money. Guardrails are the checks around an agent — input validation, output filtering, permission limits, and approval gates — that keep its autonomy inside safe bounds.

p: Validate and sanitise inputs to resist prompt injection. Constrain which tools an agent may call and with what scope. Filter or schema-check outputs before they take effect.
Least privilege applies to agents exactly as it does to users.
For consequential or irreversible actions — payments, deletions, external messages — require explicit human approval before the agent proceeds. Surface what it intends to do and why.
The goal is to automate the tedious 90% while keeping a person on the risky 10%.
key: Guardrails bound an agent's inputs, tools, and outputs
Apply least privilege to tool access
Gate irreversible actions behind human approval

takeaways: Acting agents need checks around their autonomy
Validate inputs, limit tools, filter outputs
Keep humans in the loop for consequential actions

title: Building with the Vercel AI SDK
summary: A typed, provider-agnostic toolkit for adding AI to JavaScript and TypeScript apps.
lead: The Vercel AI SDK gives JavaScript and TypeScript developers a single, typed interface over many model providers, plus first-class streaming and tool calling. Swap providers without rewriting your app, and stream responses to the UI with a few lines.

p: generateText returns a full completion; streamText streams tokens as they arrive. generateObject and streamObject return validated structured data against a schema. tool() defines functions the model can call.
Because the interface is uniform, switching from one provider to another is mostly a one-line change.
Server helpers stream model output, and framework hooks render it progressively so users see text appear immediately rather than waiting for the whole response.
Pair streamText with a schema and tools to build chat, assistants, and agents.

takeaways: The AI SDK abstracts many providers behind one typed API
generateText/streamText and generateObject cover most needs
Built-in streaming and tools make chat and agents simple

title: Vector databases for AI apps
summary: Where embeddings live, and how similarity search powers RAG and recommendations.
lead: Once you turn content into embeddings, you need somewhere to store millions of these vectors and search them by similarity in milliseconds. That is a vector database. It is the storage and retrieval engine behind RAG, semantic search, and recommendations.

p: A vector store indexes embeddings so that 'find the nearest vectors to this query' is fast even at scale, using approximate nearest-neighbour algorithms. Most also filter on metadata so you can scope a search.
Options range from dedicated services to the pgvector extension that adds vectors to Postgres you already run.
Retrieval quality depends on the embedding model, chunking strategy, and often a re-ranking pass. The database is fast; relevance is your job.
Store useful metadata alongside each vector so you can filter and cite sources.
key: Vector DBs do fast similarity search over embeddings
They power RAG, semantic search, and recommendations
pgvector adds this to Postgres without a new service

takeaways: Vector databases store and search embeddings by similarity
They are the retrieval engine behind RAG
Relevance depends on embeddings and chunking, not just the DB

title: Building a RAG pipeline end to end
summary: Assembling ingestion, retrieval, and generation into a system you can ship and improve.
lead: A working RAG feature is a pipeline with two phases. Offline, you ingest documents — load, chunk, embed, and store. Online, you handle a query — embed it, retrieve and re-rank chunks, assemble a prompt, generate, and cite. Each stage is a knob you can tune.

p: Load source documents, split them into coherent chunks sized for your model, embed each chunk, and upsert them with metadata into a vector store. Re-run this when sources change.
Chunking is the highest-leverage choice — too big buries the answer, too small loses context.

Embed the question, retrieve the top chunks, optionally re-rank them, and build a prompt that instructs the model to answer only from the provided context and cite sources. Return the answer with its references.
Add evals so you can measure whether retrieval and answers actually improve as you tune.
key: Ingestion: load, chunk, embed, store
Query: embed, retrieve, re-rank, generate, cite
Tune chunking and add evals to improve quality

takeaways: RAG is an offline ingestion plus an online query pipeline
Chunking and re-ranking drive answer quality
Instrument with evals before optimising

title: Getting reliable structured output
summary: How to make a model return clean JSON your program can trust.
lead: Conversational prose is hard for code to consume. When a program will read the model's output, you want structured data — usually JSON — that matches a known shape. The reliable approach is to define a schema, ask the model to conform to it, and validate the result.

p: Describe the exact shape you want with a schema (for example a Zod or JSON Schema definition) and use a generate-object style API or strict instructions to bind the output to it.
A schema does double duty: it guides the model and validates the response.
Even with structured-output modes, validate before use and handle failures — retry, repair, or fall back. Never assume the JSON is well-formed.
Parsing into typed objects turns a flaky text interface into a dependable one.
key: Define the output shape as a schema
Prefer object-generation APIs over parsing prose
Validate and handle malformed output

takeaways: Use schemas to get JSON a program can rely on
Schemas both guide the model and validate output
Always validate; plan for malformed responses

title: The event loop, microtasks and macrotasks
summary: Why JavaScript can be single-threaded yet handle timers, promises, and I/O without blocking.
lead: JavaScript runs your code on a single thread, but it never blocks on slow work because of the event loop. Long operations are handed off, and their callbacks are queued to run later. Understanding the queues explains the ordering surprises that trip people up.

p: After the current code finishes, the engine drains all microtasks (promise callbacks, queueMicrotask) before taking a single macrotask (a timer, an I/O callback). Then it repeats.
That is why a resolved promise's .then runs before a setTimeout(…, 0) scheduled just before it.
Awaited code resumes as a microtask, so promise chains finish before the next timer. Heavy synchronous work still blocks everything — break it up or move it off-thread.
Knowing the order lets you reason about race conditions instead of guessing.
key: Microtasks (promises) drain fully before each macrotask
await resumes as a microtask
Synchronous work still blocks the single thread

takeaways: The event loop keeps a single thread responsive
Microtasks run before the next macrotask
Long synchronous work blocks everything — split it up

title: Type coercion and equality traps
summary: The rules behind JavaScript's most infamous quirks — and how to avoid being bitten.
lead: JavaScript freely converts between types, which produces results that look bizarre until you know the rules. Most confusion comes from loose equality and implicit coercion in operators. The fixes are simple habits.

p: The == operator coerces operands before comparing, yielding oddities like 0 == '' and null == undefined being true. The === operator compares without coercion.
Default to ===; reach for == only deliberately, if ever.
The + operator means addition or string concatenation depending on operands, so 1 + '1' is '11'. Other arithmetic operators coerce to numbers, so '6' / '2' is 3.
Convert explicitly with Number(), String(), or Boolean() so intent is visible.
key: Use === to avoid coercion surprises
+ concatenates if either side is a string
Coerce explicitly to make intent clear

takeaways: Loose equality coerces; strict equality does not
+ is overloaded for strings and numbers
Convert types explicitly to avoid surprises

title: Angular signals
summary: Angular's modern reactivity primitive for fine-grained, predictable updates.
lead: Signals are Angular's reactive primitive: a value container that notifies consumers when it changes. They make change detection fine-grained — only what actually depends on a changed value updates — and the data flow easy to follow.

p: A signal holds a value you read by calling it and update with set or update. computed derives a value that recalculates only when its inputs change. effect runs side effects when the signals it reads change.
Reads are tracked automatically, so dependencies are wired without manual subscriptions.
Fine-grained updates avoid re-checking the whole component tree, improving performance and predictability over older patterns.
Signals interoperate with RxJS, so you can adopt them incrementally.
key: signal holds state; computed derives; effect reacts
Dependencies are tracked automatically on read
Updates are fine-grained, not tree-wide

takeaways: Signals are Angular's reactive value primitive
computed and effect build on tracked reads
They enable fine-grained, predictable updates

title: Express middleware and the request pipeline
summary: Everything in Express is middleware — functions chained around a request and response.
lead: An Express app is a pipeline of middleware functions, each receiving the request, the response, and a next callback. Each can read or modify req and res, end the response, or pass control onward with next(). Routing, parsing, auth, and error handling are all just middleware.

p: Middleware runs in the order you register it. Body parsers and loggers go early; route handlers in the middle; a catch-all 404 and the error handler last.
Forgetting to call next() (without ending the response) hangs the request.
An error-handling middleware has four arguments (err, req, res, next). Pass errors to it by calling next(err) from anywhere, keeping error logic in one place.
Centralising errors beats try/catch scattered through every route.
key: Middleware gets (req, res, next) and runs in order
Call next() to continue or end the response yourself
Error middleware takes four args; reach it via next(err)

takeaways: Express is an ordered pipeline of middleware
Each middleware modifies, ends, or forwards the request
Centralise errors in four-argument error middleware

title: Writing Pythonic code
summary: Idioms that make Python code shorter, clearer, and faster — the way the language wants to be written.
lead: Python rewards a particular style. Comprehensions, iteration over objects directly, context managers, and the standard library replace verbose loops and manual bookkeeping. Pythonic code is usually both more readable and faster.

p: Build lists, dicts, and sets with comprehensions instead of append loops. Iterate over items directly — for x in seq — and use enumerate or zip rather than indexing.
Generators (parentheses instead of brackets) produce items lazily, saving memory on large data.
Use with for files and locks so cleanup is automatic. Reach for collections, itertools, and dataclasses before writing them yourself.
Readable, idiomatic code is the norm reviewers expect.
key: Prefer comprehensions over manual append loops
Iterate directly; use enumerate and zip
Use with-statements and the standard library

takeaways: Comprehensions and direct iteration are idiomatic
Context managers automate cleanup
The standard library replaces most hand-rolled code

title: FastAPI fundamentals
summary: A modern Python framework where type hints generate validation and docs for free.
lead: FastAPI builds on Python type hints: you annotate your function parameters and Pydantic models, and the framework validates requests, serialises responses, and generates interactive OpenAPI docs automatically. It is async-first and fast.

p: Declare a path operation with a function whose parameters and request-body model are typed. FastAPI parses and validates input against them, returning clear errors on mismatch, with no manual checking.
The same annotations produce live Swagger documentation.
The dependency injection system supplies shared resources — database sessions, auth — to endpoints cleanly. Define endpoints with async def to handle I/O concurrently.
Pydantic models give you typed, validated data end to end.
key: Type hints generate validation and OpenAPI docs
Pydantic models define and validate request/response shapes
Dependency injection supplies shared resources

takeaways: FastAPI turns type hints into validation and docs
Pydantic models structure and check data
Async endpoints and DI keep code clean and fast

title: NumPy broadcasting and vectorisation
summary: Operate on whole arrays at once — no Python loops — by understanding broadcasting.
lead: NumPy is fast because operations run in compiled code over entire arrays rather than element-by-element in Python. Broadcasting is the rule set that lets arrays of different shapes combine without copying, and vectorisation is the habit of replacing loops with array operations.

p: When shapes differ, NumPy stretches the smaller array across the larger where a dimension is 1 or absent, without actually copying data. Adding a (3,1) column to a (1,4) row yields a (3,4) grid.
Compatible shapes line up from the trailing dimension; mismatches raise an error.
Replace per-element Python loops with whole-array expressions: arr * 2, a + b, np.where(cond, x, y). The result is shorter and often orders of magnitude faster.
If you are writing a for-loop over a NumPy array, look for the vectorised form first.
key: Broadcasting combines mismatched shapes without copying
Shapes align from the trailing dimension
Vectorised expressions replace slow Python loops

takeaways: NumPy speed comes from whole-array operations
Broadcasting stretches shapes virtually, not physically
Vectorise instead of looping in Python

title: Pandas: vectorise, do not iterate
summary: The single habit that makes Pandas fast and readable: operate on columns, not rows.
lead: Pandas wraps NumPy, so its speed comes from column-wide operations. The most common performance mistake is looping over rows with iterrows or apply when a vectorised expression would do the same job far faster and more clearly.

p: Arithmetic and comparisons work on whole Series at once: df['total'] = df['qty'] * df['price']. Boolean masks select rows: df[df['qty'] > 0]. groupby aggregates without explicit loops.
These read like the intent and run in compiled code.

sections.h: When you think you need a loop
p: Most row loops can be expressed with vectorised arithmetic, np.where, map, or groupby. Reserve apply for genuinely per-row logic, and avoid iterrows on large frames.
Reach for the vectorised form before writing a loop.
key: Operate on Series and columns, not rows
Boolean masks and groupby replace loops
Avoid iterrows on large DataFrames

takeaways: Pandas is fast when you work column-wise
Masks and groupby express row logic without loops
Vectorise before reaching for apply or iterrows

title: Polars and the lazy API
summary: A modern DataFrame library built for speed, with a lazy mode that optimises your whole query.
lead: Polars is a fast DataFrame library written in Rust, with a multi-threaded engine and an expressive API. Its standout feature is the lazy API: instead of running each step immediately, it builds a plan it can optimise before executing.

p: In eager mode each operation runs at once, like Pandas. In lazy mode you chain operations on a LazyFrame and call collect() at the end; Polars then reorders and prunes work — pushing filters down, dropping unused columns — before running it.
Lazy queries on large data are often dramatically faster.
Polars centres on expressions: pl.col('x') describes a computation that the engine can parallelise across columns and rows. They compose cleanly inside select, filter, and group_by.
Thinking in expressions, not row operations, is the key shift from Pandas.
key: Lazy mode optimises the whole query before running
collect() triggers execution of a LazyFrame
Expressions let the engine parallelise work

takeaways: Polars is a fast, multi-threaded DataFrame library
The lazy API plans and optimises before executing
Expressions replace row-by-row thinking

title: SciPy for scientific computing
summary: The toolbox that sits on NumPy for statistics, optimisation, and signal processing.
lead: SciPy extends NumPy with submodules for the heavy lifting of scientific work: statistical distributions and tests, optimisation, integration, interpolation, linear algebra, and signal processing. You import the submodule you need.

p: scipy.stats has distributions and hypothesis tests; scipy.optimize fits and minimises; scipy.integrate solves integrals and ODEs; scipy.signal filters and analyses signals; scipy.linalg handles advanced linear algebra.
Each is a focused, well-documented namespace.

title: Scikit-learn estimators and pipelines
summary: One consistent interface for classical ML — and pipelines that prevent data leakage.

title: PyTorch tensors and autograd
summary: The two ideas you need to train anything in PyTorch: tensors and automatic differentiation.
lead: PyTorch is built on tensors — NumPy-like arrays that can live on a GPU — and autograd, which records operations to compute gradients automatically. Training a model is: forward pass, compute loss, call backward, step the optimiser.

p: Tensors with requires_grad track the operations performed on them, building a graph. Calling .backward() on a loss walks that graph to fill each parameter's .grad with its gradient.
Move tensors and models to a device (CPU or GPU) for speed.

Layers like Dense, Conv2D, and LSTM cover most architectures.
Callbacks such as EarlyStopping and ModelCheckpoint hook into training to stop early or save the best weights. tf.data builds efficient input pipelines that batch, shuffle, and prefetch.
Drop to lower-level TensorFlow only when you need custom training behaviour.

title: Zod: schema validation in TypeScript
summary: Define a schema once and get both runtime validation and a static type.

title: GraphQL: ask for exactly what you need
summary: A query language for APIs where the client specifies the shape of the response.
lead: With REST, each endpoint returns a fixed shape, leading to over-fetching and many round trips. GraphQL exposes a single endpoint and a typed schema; the client sends a query describing exactly the fields it wants, and gets just those back in one request.

p: The schema defines types and the queries, mutations, and subscriptions clients may run. Each field has a resolver — a function that returns its value. The type system documents and validates the API.
Queries read, mutations write, subscriptions stream real-time updates.

title: Requests: HTTP for humans
summary: The library that made HTTP in Python simple — get, post, and handle responses without ceremony.
lead: Requests is the de facto way to make HTTP calls in Python. It wraps the messy parts of the standard library behind a clean API: a single function call sends a request, and the response object exposes status, headers, and a decoded body.

p: requests.get(url) and requests.post(url, json=data) return a Response. Read it with response.json() or response.text, and check response.status_code. Pass params= for the query string and headers= for headers.
Always call response.raise_for_status() so HTTP errors become exceptions instead of silent failures.

A Session reuses a connection and shared headers or cookies across calls, which is faster and cleaner for several requests to the same host. Set a timeout on every request so a hung server cannot freeze your program.
Never ship a request without a timeout.
key: get/post return a Response with .json(), .text, .status_code
raise_for_status turns HTTP errors into exceptions
Use a Session for repeated calls and always set a timeout

takeaways: Requests gives Python a clean HTTP API
Check status with raise_for_status and read .json()
Use Sessions and always set timeouts

title: HTTPX: requests-compatible and async-ready
summary: A modern HTTP client with the Requests API plus async support and HTTP/2.
lead: HTTPX offers an API nearly identical to Requests, so existing knowledge transfers, but adds what Requests lacks: a fully async client, HTTP/2, and strict timeouts by default. It is the natural choice for async apps and frameworks like FastAPI.

p: Use httpx.get for quick calls, or a Client for connection reuse — just like Requests. For async code, an AsyncClient exposes the same methods with await, letting you fire many requests concurrently.
The familiar surface means migrating from Requests is mostly mechanical.
HTTPX enforces timeouts unless you opt out, supports HTTP/2, and integrates cleanly with async test clients. Reuse a client rather than creating one per request.
Concurrency with AsyncClient is where it shines over Requests.
key: API mirrors Requests for an easy switch
AsyncClient enables concurrent requests with await
Timeouts are on by default; HTTP/2 is supported

takeaways: HTTPX keeps the Requests API and adds async and HTTP/2
AsyncClient runs many requests concurrently
Safer defaults like enforced timeouts

title: Scrapy: building web spiders
summary: A full framework for large-scale crawling — spiders, selectors, items, and pipelines on an async engine.
lead: Scrapy is a complete crawling framework. You write spiders that follow links across a site, extract structured items, and pass them through pipelines, all on a fast asynchronous engine.

p: A Spider defines start URLs and a parse method that yields data and follows links. Scrapy's built-in selectors query the page with CSS or XPath.
Yielding requests lets one spider crawl an entire site, page after page.
Define Items to structure extracted data, then pipelines clean, validate, and store it — to a file or database. Built-in throttling and concurrency settings keep crawls polite and efficient.
Scrapy handles retries, concurrency, and politeness so you focus on extraction.
key: Spiders crawl and parse, yielding data and new requests
CSS/XPath selectors extract fields
Items and pipelines structure and store results

takeaways: Scrapy is a framework for site-wide crawling
Spiders follow links; selectors extract fields
